attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He is not quoting anyone else here.

semantics.note: The parenthetical makes a firm claim about the past: employment effects have been more modest than some expected. Pairing it with IP-theft harm to creators matches the sentence. 'Potential' qualifies whether broader effects exist, not the comparison.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. The evaluator chose September 2026 as the period, and 'some people expected' names no forecaster, metric or place. The result depends on finding a comparable earlier expectation, which the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: Yale assessment of Oct 14, 2026 finds no clear AI labour-market footprint. This fits limited effects, but there is no observation cutoff and no earlier expectation to compare against.
Forrester company disclosure with a forecast through 2030. It says job-apocalypse fears are overstated, but gives no expectation already due by September 2026.

January 2026 advocacy summary reporting creators losing work and work scraped without consent. The underlying report was unread, so methods, observation dates and the link between copying and losses are unverified.
2025 court order: training was fair use, but pirated library copies go to trial. This bears on the appropriation element but does not measure creator harm in the assessment period.
Goldman research reports a modest net US drag concentrated on younger workers, for the past year with no exact cutoff. It includes no prior expectation to compare against.

reviews.rationale: Several sources (e1, e2, e5) suggest broad employment effects have been modest, and e3 and e4 suggest creators' work was appropriated. But no earlier expectation for a comparable measure, population and period is verified, and nothing establishes the September 2026 position or links creator losses to the copying. The evidence does not settle either part of the claim.
